source.title: When Speaker Recognition Meets Noisy Labels: Optimizations for Front-Ends and Back-Ends
source.authors: Lin Li; Fuchuan Tong; Q. Hong

record.tranche_reason: The study varies simulated label-noise rates and reports training and validation prediction accuracy over training, using speaker-recognition systems and measures rather than the original image-classification setup.
record.gate_note: The study uses closed-set label disruption up to 50%, not completely random labels. Figure 3 reports accuracy trajectories; the text describes their trends but does not provide the plotted values. Results about Front1–6 are the authors’ proposed methods, not the standard baseline. Other cited memorization findings are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study extends training-dynamics tests to speech: its baseline x-vector network learns clean data faster than corrupted data and initially learns useful representations before overfitting incorrect labels. These own results bear on V2 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: label noise degrades x-vector and PLDA performance; the proposed front-end strategies and NL-PLDA improve robustness. The authors also report early useful representation learning followed by overfitting incorrect labels during baseline training.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains speaker-recognition x-vector systems on speech with simulated closed-set, open-set, and mixed-set label noise. Its proposed systems add label-confidence training, label regularization, probability rescaling, and SubAM-Softmax; the baseline uses E-TDNN with AM-Softmax.
record.method_sensitivity: Training prediction accuracy and validation accuracy change with label-error rate and training iterations; the text describes clean data as converging faster than mislabeled data and validation accuracy degrading with further training on noisy labels.

fits_no_version.finding: Speaker-verification EER degrades with label noise, while the proposed front-end and NL-PLDA improve robustness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label corruption harms downstream speaker verification, and specialized training and back-end methods reduce that harm.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing, Vol. 30, 2022
record.problems: For training-trajectory findings, the paper gives qualitative descriptions of Figure 3 but no numerical values or uncertainty. Simulated label error rates reach 50%, not 100%; the study uses speech and speaker-recognition measures.
record.rows_left_out: No rows retained. Figure 3 describes training and validation accuracy trajectories under 0%, 20%, and 50% label error, but the plotted values are not numerically stated; the text does not provide a separate numeric result for each model and condition.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, and chance-level test error are not established; corruption reaches only 50%.
No small-constant-factor training-time estimate or explicit monotonic slowdown across corruption fractions is established.
Perfect training fit across corruption levels and test classification error rising toward chance through 100% corruption are not established.
No controlled removal of explicit regularizers or demonstration of complete random-label fitting with them.
No separate accuracy trajectories for clean and corrupted training samples or experiment with entirely random labels.

missing.what: Qualitative baseline training-dynamics evidence for V2 and V6 needs result rows. The trajectories are declared in rows_left_out, but their textual interpretation can be recorded without inventing numerical values.
missing.locator: Section V-C.1, p. 1592, Figure 3(a–c) and accompanying discussion.

record.verdict_notes: The reader incorrectly treats V6 as citation-only: Section V-C.1 supplies the study's own qualitative evidence. The supplied text omits plotted trajectory values, so neither perfect fitting nor precise convergence-time ratios can be inferred. Front2's intentionally noise-resistant behavior does not challenge the standard-network claims.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment uses a completely random labeling of the entire training set or tests chance-level test error.

The text says clean data converges faster than mislabeled data and that more iterations lead to overfitting, but it gives no training-time comparison or constant-factor estimate; the plotted trajectories are not numerically reported.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs are tested.

The study does not test corruption through 100%, nor report perfect training fit across corruption levels with test error moving toward chance. It reports speaker-recognition evaluation performance, not test classification error.
The study does not test whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
The study discusses a cited prior finding that networks learn clean patterns before memorizing noisy labels, but does not test that sequence with its own results.

relationships.condition: Baseline E-TDNN with AM-Softmax; clean versus 20% and 50% closed-set label corruption.
relationships.reason: Text accompanying Figure 3 states that clean data converges faster and mislabeled samples take longer to learn; this supports the slowdown component only. No row ids exist; verdict rests on Section V-C.1.
relationships.display_finding: Clean data converged faster than data with 20% or 50% corruption, and mislabeled examples took longer to learn.
